newsitem.title: LEBANON: Lebanon takes no chances with pope's safety.
newsitem.headline: Lebanon takes no chances with pope's safety.

text.p: The Lebanese government is mounting one of its biggest security operations since the 1975-90 civil war to guard Pope John Paul when he visits Beirut, once known as as the kidnap and murder capital of the world.
Some 20,000 Lebanese army soldiers and 5,000 troops of the Internal Security Forces will protect the pontiff during his 32-hour visit to Lebanon which starts on Saturday.

The 76-year-old pope will drive on Saturday past Shi'ite Moslem suburbs controlled by Hizbollah (Party of God), the only civil war sectarian militia not yet disbanded, on a 10 km (six miles) route to the presidential palace.

Lifesize cutouts of turbaned Shi'ite clerics including Iranian revolutionary leader Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini will stare down at the Popemobile on the airport road where a few years ago shadowy Shi'ite groups grabbed Westerners as hostages.
The pope will fly to other rendezvous outside Beirut aboard helicopters of UNIFIL, the U.N. peacekeeping force in south Lebanon, flown by Italian pilots.

Sheikh Mohammed Hussein Fadlallah, spiritual leader of Hizbollah, told the Italian newspaper La Repubblica in an interview published on Friday that Lebanon's Shi'ites were waiting for the pope with hearts filled with love and he had nothing to fear in Lebanon.
Nobody expects Shi'ite radicals to attack the pope, but Lebanon has often experienced unpleasant surprises from a variety of quarters and the Beirut government is taking no chances.

"The Lebanese army is taking full responsibility for the Pope's security during his visit. It has assigned 20,000 soldiers to fulfill this mission with tight security measures," a military source told Reuters.

"The force involved in this mission will have the support of 5,000 policemen and other security officers, 10 helicopters, 1,500 armoured vehicles, 1,000 other vehicles, four gunboats, 10 speedboats and 10 trained dogs," the source said.
Other units of the 63,000-strong army will be standing by on high alert, he said.
An operations room with representatives of the army, all other security bodies, the civil defense and Lebanese Red Cross will manage the security operation.
"The protection includes land, sea, and air patrols with bodyguards for each movement," the source said.
Beirut airport will be shut for two hours to other traffic for the pope's arrival and departure on Saturday and Sunday.
John Paul cancelled a planned visit to Beirut three years ago after a bomb explosion in a church north of Beirut in February 1994 killed 11 worshippers and injured 50.
Despite the massive security operation this time, the pope will never be far from the scenes and memories of war in Beirut.

Only 80 km (50 miles) south Hizbollah guerrillas are fighting Israeli troops occupying a south Lebanon border strip. Israeli warplanes frequently bomb them and often break the sound barrier over Beirut, just to remind the inhabitants of the capital of what they can do.

And in Beirut itself, John Paul will be a stone's throw from the former Green Line in the war-ravaged heart of the city where Moslem and Christian gunmen fought for years when he celebrates an open-air mass on the seafront on Sunday.
